paragraphs.heading: Equations that want whole numbers
paragraphs.text: A Diophantine equation is a polynomial equation whose coefficients are integers and where only integer answers count. A linear one sets a sum of unknowns, each multiplied by a coefficient, equal to a constant. An exponential one lets unknowns sit in the exponents. The name honours Diophantus of Alexandria, a Hellenistic mathematician of the 3rd century who studied such equations and was among the earliest to use symbols in algebra. The study he began is now called Diophantine analysis.

paragraphs.heading: The simplest case
paragraphs.text: The simplest linear example has the form ax + by = c, where a, b and c are given integers. It has a solution exactly when d divides c, where d = gcd (a, b). Once one solution x₀, y₀ is known, there are infinitely many, given by x = x₀ + (b/d)t and y = y₀ − (a/d)t for any integer t. Whole systems of linear equations like this can be solved with a matrix method called the Smith normal form, or with the Hermite normal form, which is much easier to compute.

paragraphs.heading: Higher powers get hard
paragraphs.text: Solving a homogeneous Diophantine equation amounts to finding the rational points of a shape called a projective hypersurface. This is usually very hard, even with only three unknowns. Fermat's Last Theorem is a witness: it says such an equation has no integer solution for degree above 2, and proving it took more than three centuries. Beyond degree three, most known results say there are no solutions or only finitely many, as in Faltings' theorem. For degree three, general methods handle almost every equation met in practice, but no known algorithm works on every cubic.

paragraphs.heading: Degree two is friendlier
paragraphs.text: Homogeneous equations of degree two are easier. The usual method has two steps: first find one solution or prove there is none, then derive all the others from it. The Hasse–Minkowski theorem decides whether a nontrivial solution exists by checking that it can be solved in the real numbers and in the p-adic numbers.

paragraphs.heading: A proof using remainders
paragraphs.text: One equation of this kind, built from squares, has no solution except (0, 0, 0), and the argument is short. We may assume x, y and z share no common factor, since dividing by it changes nothing. Squares leave a remainder of 0 or 1 when divided by 4, so the left side leaves 0, 1 or 2 and the right side 0 or 3. They can only match if x, y and z are all even, which contradicts their sharing no factor. As a result, a circle of radius √3 centred at the origin passes through no rational point.

paragraphs.heading: A limit on what can be known
paragraphs.text: Single equations have been treated as puzzles throughout history, but general theories beyond linear and quadratic equations arrived only in the twentieth century. Because these equations describe curves, surfaces and other shapes, their study also forms a part of algebraic geometry called Diophantine geometry. Hilbert's tenth problem sets a hard limit: there can be no general algorithm that decides whether an arbitrary Diophantine equation has an integer solution.
